newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ central bank chief won't go soft on inflation.
newsitem.headline: NZ central bank chief won't go soft on inflation.

text.p: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash on Thursday made strenuous efforts to dampen inflation expectations in his first major speech since a new centre-right coalition government was formed last month. Speaking to the Canterbury Employers' Chamber of Commerce, Brash said: "The Reserve Bank will be striving to keep inflation well inside the 0-3 percent range, and we best do that by trying to have inflation as close to the middle part of the range as possible."
One of the new government's first acts was to relax the bank's inflation target to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent and to add sustainable economic growth to its goal of price stability.
Last week, figures showed underlying inflation in 1996 at 2.4 percent was well ahead of economists' forecasts and well outside the old target band.

Brash said the bank had in no way had "gone soft" on inflation and would aim for the middle of the new band. He expressed concern that some people believed that by broadening the band, inflationary expectations could rise.

"Not only is there no evidence that tolerating more inflation can engineer sustainably faster real growth, there is now overwhelming evidence that high inflation positively damages the way in which the economy works," he said.

Despite the new government's directive to target sustainable growth and price stability, the bank's maximum contribution would come by maintaining the focus on a stable general level of prices, he said.
Brash also doused down expectations of sustainable growth.
"What about New Zealanders' expectations for economic growth? Are these too quite unrealistic? I believe they are, at least based on current policies and attitudes," Brash said.

Westpac Bank's Head of Financial Markets Chris Rand said Brash's comments on growth appeared to be aimed at new Treasurer Winston Peters. Peters' New Zealand First party said during last year's election campaign that it would aim for six percent growth by the end of a three-year parliamentary term, but Brash said a realistic rate was about half that.
Financial markets had anxiously awaited Brash's speech in case he had softened his famous anti-inflationary stance.

"He's emphasising that even though the target band is wider, he is going to be aiming for the middle of it. There is no basis for inflation expectations rising. He won't let things run amok," said ANZ Bank Treasurer Grant Spencer.
Higher public inflation expections were a potential cost of widening the inflation band, Spencer said.
"He's trying to minimise that by hosing expectations down."
Brash made his speech hours after Statistics New Zealand figures showed GDP grew at 0.6 percent in the September quarter against economists' average forecasts of 0.2 percent.
But they said there while there was more latent growth in some sectors of the economy, notably the service sectors, evidence remained strong that the economy was easing.
"Overall the picture is still one of an economy that is slowing," said Westpac chief economist Bevan Graham.
